slides.title: Module 2 · Direction · Unit 4
slides.notes:
UNIT 4 · DIRECTION INTEGRITY (ABCV-MBT)
Module 2 · Direction · Unit 4

UNIT INTENT
Unit 4 tests whether the chosen direction is strategically sound. 
The four ABCV checkpoints (Arena, Boundaries, Competition and Value Proposition) and their Must-Be-True conditions turn assumptions into named, verifiable conditions.

The Key Results tested are the ones the group confirmed in Unit 3: no new objective or metric enters the unit.

WHAT THE UNIT PRODUCES:
1. Each group produces its ABCV–MBT record: every Key Result it confirmed in Unit 3, taken through four steps, with one Must-Be-True condition named at each step. This is Capstone work.
2. Each participant produces two pieces of portfolio work: the Industry Illusion game of Section 2 and the Cause of Death game of Section 4.
3. Each participant writes four reflections, the last of them a closing commitment.

HOW THE UNIT RUNS:
1. You teach the whole unit from this deck first, from Section 1 to the Unit Summary. The deck is the teaching material. The teaching includes the Industry Illusion game, played with the room in groups.
2. Participants then complete their own page on the portal, in the session or after it: the reflections, their own Industry Illusion game, the group work of Section 5 and the Cause of Death game.
3. Section 5 on the portal is group work for the Capstone. The group chooses its scribe for this work.
The scribe types what the group agrees, the entries appear on every member’s page, and each member then selects Agree.
4. The Industry Illusion game in Section 2 and the Cause of Death game in Section 4 are portfolio work, completed by each participant alone.

Each slide’s notes end with a block headed "On the portal, after the teaching" wherever participants have something to complete for that part.

Your preparation as facilitator:
- Read the Facilitator Guide tab and every section of the facilitator file.
- Have the facilitator file ready in your browser at Section 2, part 2.2, so that the Industry Illusion game can be shared when you reach it.
- Each group needs its confirmed Enterprise OKRs from Unit 3 in front of it: every exercise in this unit works on those Key Results.

Where the outputs go next:
- The confirmed Must-Be-True conditions feed boxes 4A to 4D of the team’s Capstone Blueprint.

slides.title: Key learning outcomes
slides.notes:
KEY LEARNING OUTCOMES

HOW TO USE THIS SLIDE:
Read the four outcomes aloud and say where the unit delivers each one.
Outcome 1 is built in Section 1 (the four ABCV checkpoints) and produced in 5.2, where each group tests its own Key Results. 

Outcome 2 is built at each checkpoint, where a Must-Be-True condition is named, and shown in 5.1 (the worked example: one Key Result, four steps, four conditions).

Outcome 3 is built in 1.3 and 1.4 (Competition and Value Proposition) and in Section 2 (the Industry Illusion).

- Outcome 4 is built in Section 3 (the blind spot of each executive role) and produced in 5.2, where the group confirms its conditions together.

Each section slide carries that section’s two learning outcomes.

QUESTION TO ASK:
"What is your current strategy assuming about customers that nobody has verified?"

Take two or three answers. They tell you where the room expects the most from the unit.

slides.title: The unit journey
slides.notes:
FACILITATOR GUIDE · SESSION OVERVIEW

HOW TO USE THIS SLIDE:
1. Walk the five sections in one sentence each, using the list below.
2. Say plainly that Sections 1 to 3 prepare the thinking, Section 5 is where each group tests its own Key Results for the Capstone, and Section 4 is a diagnosis game each participant plays alone.
3. Tell participants how the unit runs: you teach all five sections from the deck first, and they then complete the unit on the portal, in the session or after it.

THE FIVE SECTIONS:
- Section 1 · Awareness — What: the flow from Unit 3 to Unit 4, then the four ABCV checkpoints one at a time (Arena, Boundaries, Competition, Value Proposition), each with its Must-Be-True condition, then the four brought together.

- Section 2 · Intelligence — Why: the Industry Illusion and its three traps (Familiarity, Exclusion, Complacency), then the Industry Illusion game on the case of a university.

- Section 3 · Extrapolating — Where: the ABCV checkpoint each executive role most often overlooks.

- Section 4 · Integration — Collective: Cause of Death, four failed strategies tested against the Industry Illusion.

- Section 5 · Application — In Practice: one worked example, then each group takes its Unit 3 Key Results through the same four steps.

KEY FACILITATION QUESTIONS:
- "Who else solves your customer’s problem, including those outside your industry?"
- "Which ABCV checkpoint is your executive function least likely to examine? What risk does that create for the enterprise?"
- "What is the one Must-Be-True condition your team is most likely to avoid naming, and who will verify it before the next strategic review?"

TONE AND WATCH POINTS:
- Teach: a Must-Be-True condition is written so that it is either true or false. A risk or a concern becomes a condition once it is stated as what must hold.
- Teach: competition covers every alternative the customer can choose, including doing nothing.
- Insist on specific conditions.

slides.title: Section 1 · Awareness — What
slides.notes:
SECTION 1 · AWARENESS — WHAT

HOW THIS SECTION RUNS:
1. The overview: the flow from Unit 3 to Unit 4 and the logic of the four steps.
2. 1.1 to 1.4: the four checkpoints, one at a time. Each has two slides: the checkpoint itself, then its Must-Be-True condition.
3. Bringing ABCV Together: the integrated view.
4. The Section 1 Reflections slide: the two reflections participants write on the portal after the teaching.

SECTION LEARNING OUTCOMES:
1. Assess whether measurable objectives are also strategically credible.
2. Evaluate objectives against customer value, strategic boundaries and competitive realities.

HOW TO OPEN THE SECTION:

1. Open with the question that creates the need.
Ask: "How many of you have experienced a well-crafted strategy that fell apart once execution started because of assumptions we hadn’t named until they broke?"
Pause. Use the silence.

2. Introduce ABCV–MBT.
Say: "ABCV–MBT is the tool that names those invisible assumptions before they become expensive failures."
Section intent: leaders must feel the danger of unnamed assumptions before they can value the discipline of naming them.

3. Say what each group brings into the unit.
Say: "You arrive with the Enterprise OKRs your group confirmed in Unit 3. Every exercise in this unit works on those Key Results."

slides.title: The Problem with Well-Written OKRs
slides.notes:
OVERVIEW — FROM UNIT 3 TO UNIT 4 (STRATEGIC CONTEXT)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Read the statement on the slide aloud.
"Your group has defined its OKRs. Now the question is whether they are strategically sound."

2. Say where the room stands.
Say: "In Unit 3 your group translated its Success in Practice into Enterprise OKRs.
They are measurable, they are ambitious and they have deadlines.
The next step is to move past well-written OKRs and ask whether they are strategically sound."

The GPS Analogy — Perfect Execution, Wrong Assumptions
Say:
"Have you ever followed your GPS so faithfully that even when the road starts looking suspicious, you keep driving?
The road gets narrower. The tar disappears. You pass a few goats.

But the GPS confidently announces, 'You are on the fastest route.'
And because we're committed to the destination, we keep going!
Eventually, you arrive at a locked farm gate.

Congratulations! You have executed the instructions perfectly. You are also completely lost."
(Pause for laughter.)

"That's the danger with strategy.

Your OKRs can be perfectly written.
 Your targets can be measurable. Your deadlines can be clear. 
Everyone can be accountable.
But what if the assumptions behind your chosen route are wrong?
You can achieve every milestone on the way to the wrong outcome."

Bridge to Unit 4:
"Unit 3 gave us the destination and the milestones.
In Unit 4, ABCV helps us interrogate the strategic context before we commit to the route.
Because sometimes the smartest strategic decision is to question the GPS before we run out of petrol."

slides.title: The Four ABCV Integrity Checkpoints
slides.notes:
OVERVIEW — THE LOGIC (4 STEPS · 1 CONDITION AT EACH)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Walk the four steps on the slide.
Say: "ABCV forces leaders to examine the strategic logic through four checkpoints."
- Checkpoint 1 · Define the Arena. Are we anchored in the right customer end game?
- Checkpoint 2 · Understand the Boundaries. What conditions could constrain our ability to deliver?
- Checkpoint 3 · See the Competition. Who or what else can satisfy that end game?
- Checkpoint 4 · Establish the Value Proposition. Why should the customer choose the value we create?

2. Introduce Must-Be-True, from the foot of the slide.
Say: "For each checkpoint, there has to be an underlying assumption that hold true if we are to achieve our Key results. Must-Be-True, makes the underlying assumption explicit.
It names the load-bearing walls of the goals: the specific condition that must remain true for a Key Result to survive.
If one of these conditions shifts or fails, the Key Result becomes fragile by design."

3. Show the flow from Unit 3 to Unit 4.
Say the three stages in order:
- From Unit 3: the group’s Enterprise OKRs, the Objectives and Key Results it confirmed.
- Four checkpoints: Arena, Boundaries, Competition, Value Proposition.
- Must-Be-True conditions: one at each checkpoint, for each Key Result.

Say: "No new objective and no new measure enters this unit. We test the Key Results you already hold."

4. Say what the test secures.
Say: "The test secures strategic priorities that are anchored in customer reality, designed to withstand operational constraints, positioned accurately against the competitive landscape, and coherent with the organisation’s core value.“

Say: "By naming these conditions early, you create an early-warning system that detects risks before a well-written ambition collapses under the weight of reality."

5. Bridge to 1.1.
Say: "We take the four checkpoints one at a time. We start with Arena."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants write the first reflection in Section 1 of the participant file, under the overview. It is shown on the Section 1 Reflections slide.

slides.title: 1.1 · Arena: the Customer End Game
slides.notes:
1.1 — ARENA (CUSTOMER END GAME)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Read the question of the checkpoint.
"What is the customer ultimately trying to achieve?"

2. Give the strategic logic.
Say: "Strategy starts with a shift in perspective: we compete for a customer need.
If we define our arena by our products, we miss the forest for the trees."

Say: "Arena defines the space in which value is being sought and contested."

Say: "Organisations naturally describe themselves through what they produce or the industry in which they operate: 
we are a university, 
we are a bank, 
we are a mine, 
we provide insurance.
Those descriptions tell us something important about the organisation.
They do not necessarily tell us what customer need the organisation is ultimately trying to meet."

3. Use the smartphone.
Say: "Think about the smartphone.
Inside the telecommunications industry, Nokia and Motorola were making phones.
The smartphone became a camera, a map, a bank and a personal assistant.
It moved into multiple Arenas simultaneously."

Ask: "Who in your industry is playing a different game that you’re only just starting to notice?"

Deepen, say: "Every organisation exists to do something specific for someone specific.
When it loses its sense of who it serves and what it provides, it loses the culture built around that service.
Keep the specific customer and mission visible."
(Insight: Arena · who we serve. Source: Journal, 31 January 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)

4. Teach the three depths on the slide, one at a time.
Say: "Arena deliberately returns attention to the Customer End Game. To understand that end game properly, we interrogate it at three depths."

Functional — What are they trying to achieve?
Ask: "What needs to get done, solved, accessed, changed or achieved?"
Example: A learner wants to develop relevant capability.

Experiential — What matters about how they achieve it?
Ask: "What matters to the customer about the experience of achieving the functional outcome?"
Example: For a working professional, developing capability may need to be flexible, accessible and compatible with employment.

Consequential — What does achieving it ultimately enable?
Ask: "What becomes possible, better or different for the customer once this outcome has been achieved?"
Example: A learner develops capability → to progress professionally, access opportunity or improve earning potential.

5. Read the three together.
Say: "These are three depths of one interrogation. Together, they help define the Customer End Game."


EXAMPLE
Higher education.
Functional: Build relevant and credible capability.
Experiential: Do so through learning that is flexible, accessible and compatible with work.
Consequential: Translate that capability into career progression and economic opportunity.

The Arena can therefore be expressed as: Enabling working professionals to build credible capability, in ways compatible with their working lives, that advances career and economic opportunity.

The organisation now has a much richer strategic space to interrogate than “We provide postgraduate education.”

And for that statement to hold there must an assumption that we are making which we must monitor – that working professionals continue to value personal development. at 

6. Ask the room to apply the three depths.
Ask leaders to apply the three depths to their primary customer. Online: ask them to post one line for each depth in the chat.
Listen for: the experiential and consequential depths. Most leaders find these are rarely discussed in their strategy sessions. That is the blind spot.

7. Land the line at the foot of the slide.
Read it in full: "The Industry tells you who you think you are competing with. The Arena tells you who you are actually competing with."

slides.title: 1.2 · Boundaries: the Friction Architecture
slides.notes:
1.2 — BOUNDARIES (FRICTION ARCHITECTURE)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Read the question of the checkpoint.
"What could constrain our ability to deliver within this Arena?"

2. Give the strategic logic.
Say: "Every arena has invisible walls: operational limits, regulations, or simple human resistance to change. A strategy that ignores friction is a wish."
Say: "Every strategic choice operates within conditions that enable, restrict or shape what can actually be delivered. These are Boundaries."
Key message: defining the right Arena is only the first test. The organisation must also be able to deliver within it.

3. Walk the six kinds of boundary on the slide.
- Regulatory: laws, licences, standards, accreditation.
- Operational: processes, infrastructure, capacity, supply chains.
- Technological: systems, data, interoperability, technical capability.
- Structural: governance, decision rights, organisational dependencies.
- Financial: capital, affordability, economics, funding.
- Behavioural: capability, incentives, resistance, habits, adoption.
Say: "The purpose is to find the boundaries material enough to affect the strategic outcome. A long risk register is of no use here."

4. Give the example.

EXAMPLE
Higher education. The university’s Arena requires flexible capability development for working professionals. But:
- Programme approvals take 12 months.
- Faculty contracts are designed around semesters.
- Systems require fixed annual enrolment periods.
- Accreditation limits how credentials can be structured.
These conditions reveal the friction architecture surrounding the Arena. The Arena itself still stands.

5. Ask the strategic question.
Ask: "Which conditions could materially slow, restrict or prevent us from delivering the customer end game we have defined?"

Deepen, say: "Senior teams often act on the first piece of internal data about an opportunity and miss the second-order question.
On every major opportunity, ask the question behind the question before committing."
(Insight: The question behind the question. Source: Journal, 16 May 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

6. The three types of boundaries.
Distinguish between three kinds:
- A boundary we must accept. For example, legislation.
- A boundary we can influence. Perhaps an industry standard.
- A boundary we created ourselves. Perhaps an internal process, structure or policy.

Again for each boundary – leaders must ask "What is going to push back against us? 
What internal or external friction could slow this Key Result down or stop it entirely?"
Then ask: "What must remain true operationally or regulatorily for us to actually deliver this without breaking?"
Hold out for a condition that is either true or false.

Ask: "Which of your boundaries did your own organisation create?"
Stay here. The self-created boundary generates particularly useful executive discussion.

slides.title: 1.3 · Competition: the True Landscape
slides.notes:
1.3 — COMPETITION (THE TRUE LANDSCAPE)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Read the question of the checkpoint.
"Who or what else can satisfy the same Customer End Game?"

2. Give the strategic logic.
Say: "Once you define the Arena by the customer’s need, your ‘competitors’ change.
You are fighting anyone who solves that same problem in a different way, peers included."

Say: "Competition follows Arena deliberately.
If leaders define Arena through their industry, they will probably identify competitors through their industry.
If Arena is defined around the Customer End Game, the competitive field can look very different."

3. Read the two questions on the slide, left then right.
- Who sells something similar to us?
- What alternatives does the customer have for achieving the end game? 

The critical distinction is between these two questions.

Say: "The competitor does not have to look like us, sell the same product, use the same business model or belong to the same industry.
It only needs to offer the customer a credible alternative route to the outcome."

4. Give the example.

EXAMPLE
Higher education. If we say “We provide postgraduate qualifications”, we will probably compare ourselves with other universities.
The Arena has now been defined more deeply: build credible capability, flexibly, to advance career opportunity. Who or what else can enable that? The landscape may include:
- Professional bodies.
- Corporate academies.
- Industry certifications.
- Specialist training providers.
- Digital learning platforms.
- Employer-led development.
- Alternative credential providers.

And potentially emerging models we have not historically classified as higher education.

5. Widen the list of alternatives, using the right-hand card.
Say: "Competition can also be: do it internally, do it themselves, use technology, postpone it, choose a completely different solution, or do nothing."

Ask: "Who else solves your customer’s problem, including those outside your industry?"
Listen for: competition defined as industry rivals only. Push for every alternative route the customer has to the outcome, including doing nothing.

Deepen, say: "The most effective competitive strategies target the specific assumptions on which a competitor’s position rests.
Identify the foundational assumption, and the position built on it becomes unstable."
(Insight: Competition. Source: Journal, 6 February 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

Say: Again leaders must ask what must be true for who else is meeting the customer needs for our strategy to hold.
Example, from higher education: Employers and learners must continue to perceive our credential and learning experience as sufficiently valuable to justify its additional time and cost relative to alternative capability pathways.
Say: "That assumption can be monitored. If it begins to weaken, the strategy receives an early-warning signal."

6. Land the point.
Say: "The customer is choosing between routes to an outcome."

slides.title: 1.4 · Value Proposition: Coherent Advantage
slides.notes:
1.4 — VALUE PROPOSITION (COHERENT ADVANTAGE)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Read the question of the checkpoint.
"Why should the customer choose the value we create?"

2. Give the strategic logic.
Say: "Strategy wins when you are distinct.

Every Key Result should make your unique DNA stronger.
If a goal dilutes your brand or confuses your value, it is a distraction."

Say: "Arena established what the customer is ultimately trying to achieve.
Boundaries established the conditions within which we must deliver it.
Competition revealed the alternatives available to the customer.
Value Proposition now asks: given those alternatives, why should the customer choose us?"

3. Clear away the positive attributes.
Say: "A Value Proposition is more than a description of what the organisation offers.
High quality, customer focused, innovative, excellent service, experienced people: all of these may be positive attributes.
On their own they establish no strategic value."
Ask: "What combination of value do we create that matters to this customer, in this Arena, relative to the alternatives available?"

4. Teach the three tests on the slide.

Relevance — Does it matter?
Does the value proposition address something important in the Customer End Game? If the customer does not materially value it, it is not an advantage.

Distinctiveness — Does it differentiate?
Is there something meaningfully different about the value created, or can credible alternatives make essentially the same claim?

Deliverability — Can we consistently produce it?
A promise becomes strategically valuable only when the organisation possesses the capability and system to deliver it repeatedly.

Read the foot of the slide: RELEVANT + DISTINCTIVE + DELIVERABLE = STRATEGIC VALUE.

Deepen, say: "Strategy is proven by the quality and consistency of the environment it produces.
Organisations weaken their credibility when branding, claims or public positioning exceed the quality of the lived experience."
(Insight: Value Proposition · coherence. Source: Journal, 16 July 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

5. Give the example.

EXAMPLE
S2R® EXAMPLE — RELEVANCE, DISTINCTIVENESS AND DELIVERABILITY
Say:
"Let me illustrate how we applied these three tests when developing Strategy2Results®.

1. Relevance — Does it matter?
We began by examining a persistent organisational problem: companies invest heavily in strategy development but struggle to translate strategic intent into consistent results.
We identified the Customer End Game as achieving measurable, sustained strategic results. This became the problem S2R® was designed to address.

2. Distinctiveness — Does it differentiate?
We then asked why organisations would choose S2R® when other strategy and execution solutions already exist.
We identified gaps between strategy design, functional contributions and execution discipline. This informed our DIG framework: Direction, Influence and Grounding.
We developed an integrated methodology supported by diagnostics, contribution mapping and practical execution tools. Our intended differentiation lies in connecting these elements into one coherent strategy-to-results system.

3. Deliverability — Can we consistently produce it?
We recognised that different customers need different ways to access and apply S2R®. We therefore designed three delivery models:
CESI Intensive and Flexi: Two pathways to the same professional credential, developing internal strategy integration capability.
Company Retreats: Facilitated application of S2R® by leadership teams to address real organisational challenges and produce shared strategic outputs.
Open Workshops: Focused learning experiences that develop specific strategic capabilities and practical skills.

We established IBSL to deliver these capability-development programmes, while Impactis Consulting provides organisational diagnostics, consulting interventions and digital S2R® tools.

This creates a structured foundation for consistent delivery, with repeatability to be demonstrated through client outcomes.

Close:
"Notice the sequence. We identified a problem customers genuinely care about, developed an approach intended to create distinctive value, and then designed the capabilities and delivery models needed to fulfil that promise.
That is the discipline behind testing a value proposition for Relevance, Distinctiveness and Deliverability.“

Say apply to your Key Results
Take one of the Key Results a group confirmed in Unit 3.
Ask: "How does this goal make us more ‘us’? Does this Key Result sharpen our distinctive edge or just add noise?"
Then ask: "What must remain true about our value architecture for this Key Result to stay coherent and profitable?"
Hold out for a condition that is either true or false.

slides.title: Section 1 Reflections
slides.notes:
SECTION 1 REFLECTIONS

HOW TO USE THIS SLIDE:

1. Show the slide and read the two prompts aloud.
1 · Overview reflection: "Take one Key Result your group confirmed in Unit 3. What is it assuming about the world that has not yet been verified?"

2 · Bringing ABCV Together reflection: "Which of the four ABCV checkpoints is your organisation least likely to examine rigorously before launching a new strategic initiative? What does that pattern cost you?"

2. Say what the reflection is for.
Point learners to the portal section that they will be required to complete with as much depth as possible.
The reflections build the learning portfolio they receive at the end of the programme.

Say: "You write this reflection on the portal after the teaching, with as much depth as you can."

3. Set the standard.
Say: "For the first reflection, name one real Key Result of your group and one thing it assumes. For the second, name the checkpoint and one real cost."
Listen for: an assumption stated as a worry. Ask: "Written as a condition, is it true or false today?"

4. Bridge to Section 2.
Say: "We have the four checkpoints. Section 2 asks why leaders so often fail to use them."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants write the two reflections in Section 1 of the participant file: under the overview, and under Bringing ABCV Together.

slides.title: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
slides.notes:
SECTION 2 · INTELLIGENCE — WHY

HOW THIS SECTION RUNS:
1. 2.1: the Industry Illusion and its three traps.
2. 2.2: the Industry Illusion game, played with the room in groups, from the facilitator file.
3. 2.2, after the game: the Arena question, back on the deck.

SECTION LEARNING OUTCOMES:
1. Test strategic priorities against the outcomes customers seek.
2. Surface and challenge assumptions underpinning strategic objectives.

HOW TO OPEN THE SECTION:

1. Say what the section does.
Say: "In this section you discover, through your own decisions, how an industry frame shapes what leaders notice, dismiss and trust."
Section intent: the game supplies the evidence. Arena supplies the test.

2. Read the line under the section title.
"The industry we understand becomes the boundary of the world we examine."

slides.title: 2.1 · The Industry Illusion
slides.notes:
2.1 — THE INDUSTRY ILLUSION (3 TRAPS)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

Start with the value of industry knowledge.
Say: "Industry knowledge is essential to strategy.
Over time, leaders build a deep understanding of how their industry works: its customers, competitors, economics, regulations, technologies and established ways of creating value.
That knowledge also creates a frame through which leaders interpret their environment, birthing what we call the industry illusion.

Say: "The Industry Illusion occurs when that frame becomes so familiar that leaders begin to treat it as the boundary of what is strategically relevant.“

There are three forms of industry illusion

1. Familiarity — We know this industry.
Say: "Experience creates confidence in our understanding of how the industry works.
We know the established players, customer patterns, sources of value and indicators we normally monitor.

The trap occurs when what we know becomes what we expect to continue seeing."
Strategic risk: We interpret the future through patterns established by the past.

2. Exclusion — We discount what doesn’t fit it.
Say: "Once we have a familiar picture of the industry, developments that fit that picture receive our attention.
Signals that sit outside it can appear less relevant because they do not resemble the customers, competitors, technologies or business models we associate with our industry.

The trap is that we may see the signal but exclude it from serious strategic consideration."
Strategic risk: What does not fit our industry frame gets underestimated.

3. Complacency — We become confident in the world we can see.
Say: "When the organisation continues to perform, our established view of the industry appears to be validated.
Market position, reputation, customer demand or past success can reinforce the belief that we understand what matters.

The trap occurs when evidence of current success becomes reassurance about future relevance."
Strategic risk: We continue looking in the same places because nothing has yet forced us to look elsewhere.

Bridge to the game.
Say: "You are about to make three decisions as an executive team. Make each one as you would at work."

slides.title: 2.2a · The Industry Illusion Game
slides.notes:
2.2 — THE INDUSTRY ILLUSION GAME: THE FUTURE OF A UNIVERSITY (3 ROUNDS)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Share the game.
Stop sharing the deck and share the browser window that holds the facilitator file, at Section 2, part 2.2.
Have that page ready before the lesson begins.
The page holds six steps in order: Case Brief, Round 1, Round 2, Round 3, The Reveal, Apply Arena.
Play the game with the room in groups. Each group makes its decision and defends it.
Important: do not tell participants which trap each round is testing. Do not correct their answers during the game. Capture their decisions. Reveal the traps only at the end.

2. Give the case brief.
Say: "You are the executive team of Apex University, an established private university."
Read the brief on the screen: 18,000 students; strong undergraduate and postgraduate programmes; recognised accreditation; a respected business school; growing online delivery; strong relationships with employers; good graduate employment outcomes; stable enrolment.
Say: "The Board is beginning development of the university’s 2032 Strategy.
Your task is to advise the Board on where it should focus its strategic attention."

3. Round 1 — Where would you look?
Say: "You have been asked to understand how Apex University’s environment is changing. Where would you look for intelligence?"
Show the eight intelligence sources, A to H, on the screen.
Say: "Select four that you would prioritise."
Each group posts its four letters in the chat. Record the choices.
What this round tests, for you only: Familiarity. Do participants gravitate toward A to D because these are recognisably higher-education indicators? Do not reveal this.

4. Round 2 — What deserves attention?
Say: "Your strategy team has brought six developments to the executive committee. You only have capacity to investigate three in depth."
Show the six signals on the screen.
Ask: "Which three warrant immediate strategic investigation?"
Then ask: "Which three would you deprioritise?"
Require each group to make the decision. Capture what it excluded and, importantly, why.
What this round tests, for you only: Exclusion. Are signals 3, 4 and 6 discounted because they do not initially look like developments inside higher education? Do not reveal the trap.

5. Round 3 — Should we be worried?
Show the Apex University performance report on the screen: enrolment +5%, revenue +7%, graduate employment 86%, accreditation strong, student satisfaction 82%, market position top 3 private university, online enrolment +12%.
Say: "The Board asks whether the university needs to reconsider its fundamental strategic direction."
Give the three choices: A, no major change; B, adjust; C, re-examine. Each group must select one and defend it.
What this round tests, for you only: Complacency. Does strong current performance reassure participants that the university understands its future? Choice A is a reasonable answer on the page: the numbers genuinely look good.

6. The Reveal.
Now return to their decisions, round by round.
Round 1, where did you look? Reveal Familiarity: We know this industry.
Ask: "How much of your attention went toward the world you already recognised as higher education?"
Round 2, what did you exclude? Reveal Exclusion: We discount what doesn’t fit it.
Ask: "Which signals did you deprioritise because they appeared to sit outside the conventional higher-education environment?"
Round 3, what reassured you? Reveal Complacency: We become confident in the world we can see.
Ask: "Did strong current performance influence how urgently you believed the university needed to question its future?"
Then give the crucial insight.
Say: "Apex did not lack information. The question is what its industry frame caused leaders to notice, dismiss and trust."

7. Return to the deck.
Stop sharing the facilitator file and return to the deck. The next slide carries the Arena question.

AFTER THE SESSION:
Each participant’s own game reaches you with the submission, under the heading Industry Illusion Game.

slides.title: Section 3 · Extrapolating — Where
slides.notes:
SECTION 3 · EXTRAPOLATING — WHERE

HOW THIS SECTION RUNS:
1. 3.1a: the nine executive roles and the checkpoint each most often overlooks.
2. 3.1b: one role card in full, the CEO.
3. The Section 3 Reflections slide: the reflection participants write on the portal after the teaching.

SECTION LEARNING OUTCOMES:
1. Diagnose integrity blind spots arising from functional perspectives.
2. Assess how functional blind spots combine into enterprise strategic risk.

HOW TO OPEN THE SECTION:

1. Say what the section does.
Say: "Every executive role is trained to protect a different part of the enterprise system.
These specialisations create selective attention, and predictable strategic blind spots across the leadership mandate."
Section intent: make the ABCV framework personal to each leader’s role. The aim is illumination. Leaders should finish knowing which ABCV checkpoint is most likely their organisational blind spot and why it creates specific downstream consequences.

2. Return to the answers from Section 1.
Recall the checkpoints the room named as most consistently overlooked at the end of Section 1. Section 3 shows where those answers come from.

slides.title: 3.1a · The Executive Hot Zone
slides.notes:
3.1 — THE EXECUTIVE HOT ZONE: ROLE-BASED BLIND SPOTS (9 ROLES)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

The elephant story and biases will always show up as leaders give their input to the strategy.

And what we is that the biases show up on the basis of the role the leader holds more than their character.

Say:
"Every executive looks at strategy through the eyes of their responsibility. That view gives them expertise, but it can also create blind spots.
Let's examine four executives. Each is competent, each is doing their job, and each may still overlook something important about the organisation's strategic context.“

2. Walk through the four characters

CEO — Blind Spot: Boundaries
"The CEO sees the vision and wants the organisation to move. But sometimes the excitement about where we are going overshadows the conditions that could prevent us from getting there.
The ABCV question becomes: What boundaries could prevent us from achieving our strategic ambition, and which can we influence or redesign?"

CFO — Blind Spot: Arena
"The CFO examines financial viability, revenue, costs and returns. The numbers may look healthy, but financial performance often tells us what has happened. It says less about whether the underlying customer need is changing.
An organisation can continue generating revenue from a business model whose relevance is gradually declining.
The ABCV question becomes: Are we still operating in an arena where the customer need is important, relevant and sustainable?"

CHRO — Blind Spot: Competition
"The CHRO focuses on people capability, engagement and alignment. These are essential to execution.
But imagine having highly motivated employees, excellent teamwork and strong performance management, all directed towards a strategy that competitors are already making irrelevant.
The ABCV question becomes: Are we building and aligning our people's capabilities to compete effectively in the market we are targeting?"

CTO — Blind Spot: Value Proposition
"The CTO may focus on technological capability, system performance and innovation.
We can build a sophisticated digital platform, automate processes and introduce advanced technology. But technological excellence does not automatically translate into customer value.
The ABCV question becomes: Does our solution create value customers genuinely care about, and is that value meaningfully different from available alternatives?"

3. Draw Out the Strategic Insight
Say:
"Notice something interesting. None of these executives is necessarily wrong.
The CEO is right to pursue the vision. The CFO is right to protect financial viability. The CHRO is right to develop people. The CTO is right to strengthen technological capability.

The problem emerges when each executive's functional perspective becomes the organisation's entire strategic perspective.
That is how we can end up with a strategy that makes perfect sense within individual functions but fails when tested against the broader strategic context."

4. Engage Participants
Ask:
"Looking at these four characters, which blind spot do you recognise most in your organisation?"
Take two or three responses.
Then ask:
"Can you think of a situation where an executive was making a perfectly reasonable decision from their functional perspective, but that decision created a problem for the wider organisation?"

5. Close and Reinforce
Say:
"This is why ABCV matters.
Boundaries, Arena, Competition and Value Proposition help us examine strategic direction from perspectives that individual functions may overlook.
And remember, these are illustrative blind spots. A CEO could overlook competition, a CFO could overlook boundaries, and a CTO could overlook the arena.
The lesson is that functional expertise gives us depth, but strategic integration gives us the enterprise view.
When we bring these perspectives together, we improve our ability to identify the assumptions, constraints and competitive realities that could undermine our strategy before we commit to execution."
Final reflection:
"Which part of ABCV would your own functional expertise naturally lead you to overlook?"

slides.title: Section 3 Reflections
slides.notes:
SECTION 3 REFLECTIONS

HOW TO USE THIS SLIDE:

1. Show the slide and read the prompt aloud.
3.1 Reflection: "Having explored your role’s typical blind spot: what is one MBT condition in that checkpoint that your organisation is currently assuming without confirmation? What would it take to verify it?"

2. Say what the reflection is for.
Point learners to the portal section that they will be required to complete with as much depth as possible.
The reflections build the learning portfolio they receive at the end of the programme.

Say: "You write this reflection on the portal after the teaching, with as much depth as you can."

3. Set the standard.
Say: "Name the checkpoint of your role.
Write one condition your organisation is assuming, in a form that is either true or false.
Then say what evidence would verify it and who holds that evidence."
Listen for: a general concern where a condition is needed. Ask: "What exactly must remain true?"

4. Bridge to Section 5.
Say: "We know the checkpoints and we know our blind spots. Section 5 applies both to your own Key Results."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants write the reflection in Section 3 of the participant file: 3.1 Reflection.

slides.title: Section 4 · Integration — Collective
slides.notes:
SECTION 4 · INTEGRATION — COLLECTIVE

HOW THIS SECTION RUNS:
1. Cause of Death: how the game is played.
2. The four mines.
3. The Section 4 Reflections slide: the closing commitment.
4. The Unit Summary.

SECTION LEARNING OUTCOMES:
1. Diagnose failures of directional integrity in realistic strategic situations.
2. Select integrity checks that would prevent or reduce identified strategic failures.

HOW TO OPEN THE SECTION:

1. Say what the section does.
Say: "You now apply ABCV diagnostic thinking under pressure.
Each scenario is a real-world strategy failure in which an Industry Illusion kept leaders from seeing the breakdown."
Section intent: participants find the illusion first, then the ABCV checkpoint where that illusion sits.

2. Say who plays.
Say: "Each of you plays this game alone, on the portal, after the teaching. It is portfolio work."

slides.title: Cause of Death · Match the Breakdown
slides.notes:
CAUSE OF DEATH — MATCH THE BREAKDOWN (2 PARTS · PORTFOLIO WORK)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Explain the two parts on the slide.
Say: "Each scenario is answered in two parts. First you find the illusion. Then you find where it sits."
- Find the illusion: the participant chooses the investigation question the scenario answers. Each question reveals one illusion.
- Find where it sits: the participant chooses the ABCV checkpoint the illusion hid from leaders: Arena, Boundaries, Competition or Value Proposition.

2. Read the three investigation questions.
- Question 1: What did leaders expect to continue seeing because it was what they already knew?
- Question 2: Which signal did leaders see and then discount because it did not fit their established picture?
- Question 3: Which evidence of current success did leaders treat as reassurance about the future?
Do not say which illusion each question reveals. The participants work that out.

3. Explain the mine.
Say: "When both parts are right, the mine is defused.
A wrong answer detonates it: you read the hint and try again.
A mine defused at the first attempt earns 2 points, at a later attempt 1 point.
The maximum is 8."
Say: "The same illusion can sit behind more than one mine."

4. Set the standard.
Say: "Say your reasoning to yourself before you answer. Guessing the right checkpoint for the wrong reason will surface."

slides.title: Section 4 Reflections
slides.notes:
SECTION 4 REFLECTIONS

HOW TO USE THIS SLIDE:

1. Show the slide and read the prompt aloud.
Closing Commitment: "What is one MBT condition your organisation is currently avoiding naming? Why? What will you do about it before your next strategic review?"

2. Say what the reflection is for.
Point learners to the portal section that they will be required to complete with as much depth as possible.
The reflections build the learning portfolio they receive at the end of the programme.

Say: "You write this reflection on the portal after the teaching, with as much depth as you can."

3. Set the standard.
Say: "Name one condition, in a form that is either true or false.
Say why it is being avoided.
Then name one action and the date of your next strategic review."

Deepen, say: "The instinct to manage the appearance of a known exposure, and leave the exposure itself unaddressed, turns a survivable warning into a failure.
A risk that has been named and then avoided chooses its own moment.
Treat a clear warning as a directive to act."
(Insight: Named and avoided. Source: Journal, 16 June 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants write the Closing Commitment at the end of Section 4 of the participant file.

slides.title: Section 5 · Application — In Practice
slides.notes:
SECTION 5 · APPLICATION — IN PRACTICE

HOW THIS SECTION RUNS:
1. 5.1: the worked example. One Key Result of the client services company from Unit 3, taken through four steps, on six slides.
2. 5.2: the briefing for the Capstone work. Each group takes its own Unit 3 Key Results through the same four steps.
3. 5.3: verification ownership and the executive blind spot. The group assigns each critical condition to an executive and names the checkpoint its team is most likely to overlook.

SECTION LEARNING OUTCOMES:
1. Validate the critical assumptions, dependencies and uncertainties behind strategic objectives.
2. Assign and coordinate executive accountability for validating strategic conditions.

HOW TO OPEN THE SECTION:

1. Say what the section does.
Say: "This is where the checkpoints are applied to your own direction.
Your group brings in the Key Results it confirmed in Unit 3 and takes each one through four steps.
At each step it names the condition that must remain true."
This is Capstone work: the confirmed outputs feed each team’s Capstone Blueprint.

2. Say the order.
Say: "We first walk one worked example in full. Your exercise then follows the worked example step for step."

slides.title: 5.1 · Worked Example: Stress-Testing a Key Result
slides.notes:
5.1 — WORKED EXAMPLE: STRESS-TESTING A KEY RESULT (4 STEPS)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Recall the company.
Say: "This example continues the client services company you met in Unit 3, part 2.2."
Its Success in Practice reads: “We will be the service partner our clients rely on first, by ensuring every client experiences fast, consistent and effortless service.”

2. Read the Key Result on the slide aloud.
Objective: Deliver consistently fast and effortless service experiences for customers
Key Result: Reduce average response time to customer requests from 12 hours to 4 hours by 30 June 2027

3. Say how the example runs.
Say: "The company takes this one Key Result through the four steps. Each step ends with the condition that must remain true for the Key Result to hold."
At the end of each step, read the Must-Be-True condition aloud and ask what it would look like if it failed. Each condition is either true or false.

slides.title: 5.1 · Step 1: Define the Arena
slides.notes:
5.1 — WORKED EXAMPLE · STEP 1: DEFINE THE ARENA

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Read the question of the step from the slide.
"Which customer need does “Reduce average response time to customer requests from 12 hours to 4 hours by 30 June 2027” serve: functional, experiential or consequential?"

2. Read the company’s answers.
Functional · What does the customer need done that this Key Result serves? Have a service request answered and resolved.
Experiential · What matters to the customer about how it is done? Fast and effortless: one contact, no chasing.
Consequential · What does this Key Result enable for the customer? Keep their own operations running and their commitments to their own customers met.

3. Read the Must-Be-True condition.
The question: "What must remain true about that functional, experiential or consequential need for “Reduce average response time to customer requests from 12 hours to 4 hours by 30 June 2027” to stay relevant?"
The condition: Experiential: clients continue to rank speed of response among their top three reasons for choosing a service partner.
Ask: "What would we see first if clients stopped ranking speed of response among their top three reasons?"

4. Point out the depth.
Say: "The condition rests on the experiential depth. The company says so in the first word."

slides.title: 5.1 · Step 2: Understand the Boundaries
slides.notes:
5.1 — WORKED EXAMPLE · STEP 2: UNDERSTAND THE BOUNDARIES

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Read the question of the step from the slide.
"Which conditions could materially slow, restrict or prevent us from delivering “
Reduce average response time to customer requests from 12 hours to 4 hours by 30 June 2027”?"

2. Read the company’s answers.
The slide lists four boundaries. For each one, give its kind and say whether the company must accept it, can influence it, or created it itself:
- Requests that cross Commercial, Operations and Customer Service wait at each handover. Operational · Created ourselves.
- Front-line staff lack the authority and the client information to answer alone. Behavioural · Created ourselves.
- Each function records requests in its own system, with no shared view. Technological · Created ourselves.
- Request volumes peak at month-end. Operational · Must accept.

3. Read the Must-Be-True condition.
The question: "What must remain true operationally or regulatorily for us to deliver “Reduce average response time to customer requests from 12 hours to 4 hours by 30 June 2027” without breaking?"
The condition: Handovers between Commercial, Operations and Customer Service are completed inside four hours.
Ask: "What would we see first if handovers took longer than four hours?"

4. Point out the pattern.
Say: "Three of the four boundaries were created by the company itself. Those are the ones it can remove."

slides.title: 5.1 · Step 3: See the Competition
slides.notes:
5.1 — WORKED EXAMPLE · STEP 3: SEE THE COMPETITION

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Read the question of the step from the slide.
"Who or what else can give the customer what “Reduce average response time to customer requests from 12 hours to 4 hours by 30 June 2027” delivers?"

2. Read the company’s answers.
The slide lists five alternatives:
- Rival client services firms.
- Larger providers with round-the-clock service desks.
- The client’s own in-house team.
- Self-service tools that answer simple requests at once.
- Doing nothing: the client lives with a slower answer.

3. Read the Must-Be-True condition.
The question: "What must remain true about the advantage “Reduce average response time to customer requests from 12 hours to 4 hours by 30 June 2027” gives us compared to these other options?"
The condition: A four-hour response remains faster than rival firms and clients’ in-house options provide.
Ask: "Which of the five alternatives would close the gap first?"

4. Point out the width of the list.
Say: "Two of the five alternatives sit outside the industry, and one is doing nothing."

slides.title: 5.1 · Step 4: Establish the Value Proposition
slides.notes:
5.1 — WORKED EXAMPLE · STEP 4: ESTABLISH THE VALUE PROPOSITION

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Read the question of the step from the slide.
"What about “Reduce average response time to customer requests from 12 hours to 4 hours by 30 June 2027” will make customers choose us?"

2. Read the company’s answers.
Relevant · Does this Key Result matter to the customer? Speed of response is among the main reasons clients choose a service partner.
Distinctive · What does it give the customer that the alternatives do not? One joined-up team answers the request. Larger providers pass it between departments.
Deliverable · Can we consistently produce it? Cross-functional execution routines and named owners make a four-hour response repeatable.

3. Read the Must-Be-True condition.
The question: "What must remain true about our value architecture for “Reduce average response time to customer requests from 12 hours to 4 hours by 30 June 2027” to stay coherent and profitable?"
The condition: Faster response is delivered with no loss in the quality of the answer the client receives.
Ask: "What would clients notice first if speed came at the cost of the quality of the answer?"

slides.title: 5.1 · Four Steps, Four Conditions
slides.notes:
5.1 — WORKED EXAMPLE: FOUR STEPS, FOUR CONDITIONS

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Read the four conditions in order.
- Arena: Experiential: clients continue to rank speed of response among their top three reasons for choosing a service partner.
- Boundaries: Handovers between Commercial, Operations and Customer Service are completed inside four hours.
- Competition: A four-hour response remains faster than rival firms and clients’ in-house options provide.
- Value Proposition: Faster response is delivered with no loss in the quality of the answer the client receives.

2. Land the line at the foot of the slide.
Say: "Four steps, four conditions. If one of them shifts or fails, the Key Result becomes fragile by design."

3. Test the standard.
Ask: "Could someone outside this company verify each of these four conditions?"
Say: "That is the standard for your own conditions: specific enough that someone else could attempt to verify them."

Deepen, say: "A decision can solve today’s problem while creating future instability.
Assess each objective by the capability, dependency, risk and future consequence it creates."
(Insight: Today’s fix, tomorrow’s cost. Source: Journal, 19 July 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

4. Bridge to 5.2.
Say: "Your exercise is this example repeated on your own Key Results: the same four steps, in the same order."

slides.title: 5.2b · Stress Test Your Key Results: the Four Steps
slides.notes:
5.2 — STRESS-TESTING YOUR KEY RESULTS · THE FOUR STEPS (CAPSTONE WORK)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

Explain how the group works, using the four lines on the slide.
Say: "Your group agrees each entry.
The group chooses its scribe, who types the agreed wording.
The entries appear on every member’s page, and each member then selects Agree."

Say what the group works on.
Say: "Your group does for its own Key Results what the worked example did.
Your confirmed Key Results from Unit 3 are already listed on your page.
No new objective or measure is added."

Say what follows.
Say: "When every Key Result has been taken through the four steps, your group goes on to 5.3."


Walk the four steps on the slide. Each one is taken for one Key Result at a time.
Step 1 · Define the Arena. The group says which customer need the Key Result serves, at three depths (functional, experiential, consequential). Then names what must remain true about that need.

Step 2 · Understand the Boundaries. The group lists the boundaries material enough to slow, restrict or prevent delivery of the Key Result, with the kind of each and whether it must be accepted, can be influenced or was created by the organisation itself. Then it names what must remain true for delivery.

Step 3 · See the Competition. The group lists who or what else can give the customer what the Key Result delivers, including alternatives outside the industry and doing nothing. Then it names what must remain true about its advantage.

Step 4 · Establish the Value Proposition. The group says what about the Key Result will make customers choose the organisation, using the three tests (relevant, distinctive, deliverable). Then it names what must remain true about its value architecture.


2. Say how the questions read on the page.
Say: "On your page every question names your own Key Result, word for word. You answer about that Key Result and no other."

3. Set the standard for a condition.
Say: "The condition your group names must be specific enough that someone else could attempt to verify it.
“The market must support us” becomes a condition once it names what must be true, for whom and by when.
"
How each condition is written: as a statement that is either true or false. The group restates a risk or a concern as the condition that must hold.
Where a group cannot name a condition: the Key Result itself may be insufficiently grounded. The group asks itself what that tells it about the Key Result.
Ask: "If you cannot name a Must-Be-True, what does that tell you about this Key Result?"


Lead into 5.3 with the question it answers.
Ask: "Which one MBT condition, if left unverified, represents the greatest risk to our strategy’s integrity? Who is responsible for that verification?"

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants work in their groups in 5.2 of the participant file. This is Capstone work.
1. The group’s confirmed Key Results from Unit 3 are listed in 5.2.
2. The group takes one Key Result through the four steps and names the condition at each step.
3. The group takes the next Key Result through the same four steps, until every Key Result is complete.
4. A record shows the condition named at each step for every Key Result. The group then goes on to 5.3.

AFTER THE SESSION:
The record reaches you with each participant’s submission, under the heading ABCV–MBT: Stress-Testing the Key Results.
The confirmed conditions feed boxes 4A to 4D of the team’s Capstone Blueprint.

slides.title: 5.3 · Verification Ownership and Executive Blind Spots
slides.notes:
5.3 — VERIFICATION OWNERSHIP AND EXECUTIVE BLIND SPOTS (CAPSTONE WORK)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Say why ownership matters.
Say: "Each Must-Be-True condition your group named in 5.2 holds only while someone checks it.
In 5.3 your group assigns each check to an executive."

2. Teach verification ownership.
Say: "For each critical condition, name the executive accountable for verifying it, the evidence that will confirm it still holds, and the date of the first check."
One executive owns each check, with evidence someone else could inspect and a date.

3. Teach the executive blind spot.
Say: "Section 3 showed that each executive role tends to overlook one checkpoint.
Look around your table: which checkpoint is your executive team most likely to overlook? What is the enterprise risk if it does?"

4. Ask the question 5.3 answers.
Ask: "Which one MBT condition, if left unverified, represents the greatest risk to our strategy’s integrity? Who is responsible for that verification?"

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants work in their groups in 5.3 of the participant file. This is Capstone work, typed by the group’s scribe.
1. The group reads its Must-Be-True conditions from 5.2, listed in 5.3.
2. For each critical condition, the group names the executive accountable, the evidence and the date of the first check.
3. The group selects the checkpoint its executive team is most likely to overlook, and states the enterprise risk.
4. Each participant reads the record and selects Agree. Print gives a copy of the record.

AFTER THE SESSION:
The record reaches you with each participant’s submission, under the heading ABCV–MBT: Stress-Testing the Key Results.
The agreed work feeds boxes 4A to 4F of the team’s Capstone Blueprint: the conditions in 4A to 4D, verification ownership in 4E and the executive blind spot in 4F.

slides.title: Unit Summary · The closing question
slides.notes:
UNIT SUMMARY (UNIT 4 SYNTHESIS)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Recap the unit, section by section.
Say: "This session was about ensuring strategic direction is structurally sound before the first move of execution is made.
The ABCV–MBT framework served as our strategic integrity filter."
- 1 · Awareness: a well-written OKR can still rest on unnamed conditions. ABCV examines the strategic logic at four checkpoints, and a Must-Be-True condition at each makes the underlying assumption explicit.
- 2 · Intelligence: industry knowledge becomes a frame, and three reinforcing traps (Familiarity, Exclusion and Complacency) turn that frame into the boundary of the world leaders examine.
- 3 · Extrapolating: every executive role sees through a specialised perspective, and each has a checkpoint it most often overlooks.
- 4 · Integration: in Cause of Death each participant tests four failed strategies against the Industry Illusion.
- 5 · Application: each group takes the Key Results it confirmed in Unit 3 through four steps, names the condition that must remain true at each step, assigns each critical condition to an executive and names the checkpoint its team is most likely to overlook.

2. Ask the closing question on the slide.
Ask: "What is the one MBT condition your team is most likely to avoid naming? Why? And what will you do about it before the next strategic review?"
Take an answer from each group.

3. Close the unit.
Say: "The ABCV–MBT checkpoints turn your OKRs from polished aspirations into resilient execution signals, grounded in the hard realities of the enterprise system."

4. Say what happens on the portal.
Say: "You now complete the unit on the portal: your reflections, your own Industry Illusion game, your group’s work in Section 5, Cause of Death and your closing commitment.
When your page is complete, you submit the unit."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants complete every part of the participant file and submit the unit to the facilitator from the end of Section 4.

AFTER THE SESSION:
Each submission reaches you in the facilitator dashboard.
The group’s agreed Section 5 work feeds boxes 4A to 4F of the team’s Capstone Blueprint.
